'''Jerry Gallwas''' (born 1936) is an American rock climber active in the 1950s during the dawn of the Golden Age of Yosemite [[Rock climbing|Rock Climbing]].<ref>Denny, Glen, Yosemite in the Sixties, Patagonia and T. Adler Books, 2007 {{ISBN|9780979065903}}</ref><ref>Roper, Steve, Ed., Ordeal by Piton Writings From the Golden Age of Yosemite Climbing, Stanford University Libraries, 2003, {{ISBN|0-911221-26-3}}.</ref> He achieved a number of pioneering first ascents including [[sandstone]] spires in the American Southwest, and the [[first ascent]] of the Northwest Face of [[Half Dome]] with [[Royal Robbins]] and Mike Sherrick in 1957. Gallwas made his own heat-treated chrome-molybdenum steel alloy [[piton]]s, which contributed to the success of the climb.

Gallwas studied chemistry at [[San Diego State University]] and spent much of his career working for scientific instrument maker [[Beckman Instruments]], Inc. He helped to develop consensus standards for laboratory medicine, and served on the board of directors and as president of the [[Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute|National Committee for Clinical Laboratory Standards]].

== Early life ==
Gerald Ernst (Jerry) Gallwas was born in [[Whittier, California]], the only child of Ernst and Lois Gallwas. Gallwas' father held many jobs, including farmer, iron worker, and commercial fisherman. His mother was a schoolteacher. Both parents were outdoor enthusiasts.{{citation needed|date=November 2019}}

Gallwas, a native of California,  first showed an interest in climbing in junior high school. Using a [[Sierra Club]] publication drawing as a guide, he practiced rappelling on a hemp rope.<ref>Brower, David R., Ed., p.164, Manual of Ski Mountaineering, Brower, Second Edition, University of California Press, Berkeley and Los Angeles 1947.</ref>

In 1950, Gallwas and his family vacationed in [[Yosemite National Park]]. On the front of Best Studio, now the [[Ansel Adams Gallery]], Gallwas spied a picture of [[John Salathé]] standing on the tip of the [[Lost Arrow Spire|Lost Arrow]] taking a photograph of his climbing partner, Anton Nelson, as Nelson was rappelling.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ansel Adams |url=http://www.yosemiteclimbing.org/ansel-adams |website=Yosemite Climbing Association |accessdate=26 June 2020}}</ref><ref name="CCP">{{cite web |title=Ansel Adams 1902 - 1984, First Ascent of the Lost Arrow |url=https://ccp.arizona.edu/images/849175 |website=Center for Creative Photography, Part of The University of Arizona |accessdate=10 June 2020}}</ref> Gallwas imagined one day taking a photo where Salathé stood.{{citation needed|date=November 2019}} In 1954, Gallwas fulfilled that dream by completing the 5th ascent of the spire with Wayne Merry.<ref>Schutt, Art, Yosemite Climbs, The Mugelnoos* No.258, p.1, June 10, 1954.</ref>

== Climbing experiences==

In 1951, Gallwas began climbing with members of the Sierra Club from Southern California, including [[Royal Robbins]] and Don Wilson. The three became known as "The Southern Californians" to distinguish them from other California climbing groups. Gallwas described his relationship with Robbins and Wilson as teenage amateurs in tennis shoes. At [[Tahquitz Rock|Tahquitz]] (Lily Rock), the three honed their skills and dreamed of big climbs to come.<ref>Jones, Chris, Climbing in North America, pp.197-211, University of California Press, Berkeley, Lost Angeles, London, 1976, {{ISBN|0-520-02976-3}}.</ref><ref>Wilts, Charles, Ed., Climber's Guide to Tahquitz and Suicide Rocks, The American Alpine Club, Inc., New York, 1979, {{ISBN|0-930410-07-6}}.</ref>

The vision started to become a reality when, in 1953, the three made the second ascent of the North Wall of [[Sentinel Rock]].<ref name="Isserman"/>{{rp|311}}<ref>Robbins, Royal, Fail Falling, My Life, Vol. II, pp. 79-91, Pink Moment Press, California 2010, {{ISBN|978-0-9825000-2-6}}.</ref><ref>Roper, Steve, Camp 4 Recollections of a Yosemite Rockclimber, p.58, The Mountaineers, Seattle, 2004, {{ISBN|0-89886-587-5}}.</ref> Robbins showed little interest in desert climbing, so Gallwas teamed with Wilson and Mark Powell to make a series of pioneering first ascents of sandstone spires in the American Southwest. These included [[Spider Rock]], Cleopatra's Needle, and the [[Totem Pole (Monument Valley)|Totem Pole]].<ref name="Isserman"/>{{rp|327–328}}<ref>Wilson, Don M., The First Ascent of Spider Rock, Vol. 42, No.6, Sierra Club Bulletin, June 1957.</ref><ref>Wilson, Don, Cleopatra's Needle, Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 42, No.6, pp. 63-64, June 1957.</ref><ref>Wilson, Don, The Totem Pole, Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 43, No. 9, p. 72, November 1958.</ref><ref>Bartlett, Steve "Crusher" (2010), Desert Towers: Fat Cat Summits and Kittle Litter Rock, pp. 37-50, Boulder, CO, USA, Sharp Edge Publishing LLC, 2010, {{ISBN|978-1-892540-70-6}}.</ref><ref name="Isserman">{{cite book |last1=Isserman |first1=Maurice |title=Continental divide : a history of American mountaineering |date=2016 |publisher=W. W. Norton & Company |isbn=978-0-393-06850-4 |edition=First |url=https://labor.history.ucsb.edu/sites/secure.lsit.ucsb.edu.hist.d7_labor/files/sitefiles/ContinentalDivide-Ch6.pdf |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref> Bill Feuerer joined Gallwas, Wilson, and Powell on the Totem Pole ascent. Gallwas' final major ascent was the Northwest Face of [[Half Dome]] in the summer of 1957. On this climb, he teamed with Royal Robbins and Mike Sherrick.<ref name="Isserman"/>{{rp|312–316}}<ref>Sherrick, Michael P., The Northwest Face of Half Dome, Vol. 43, No. 9, 1958, pp. 19-23, Sierra Club Bulletin.</ref><ref>Fidelman, Dean and Long, John, Eds. Yosemite in the Fifties, The Iron Age, pp. 47-50, Patagonia, Ventura, 2015, {{ISBN|978-1-938340-48-2}}.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Royal Robbins And The First Ascent Of Half Dome  |date=April 18, 2017 |url=https://www.adirondackexplorer.org/outtakes/royal-robbins-first-ascent-half-dome |website=Adirondack Explorer |accessdate=4 June 2020}}</ref> The [[Regular Northwest Face of Half Dome]] ascent was the first Grade VI climb in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Yosemite National Park Climbing Rangers and Park Geologist |title=Half Dome Post-Rock Fall Conditions: One Year Later |date=     Oct 20, 2016 |url=https://www.climbing.com/news/half-dome-post-rock-fall-conditions-one-year-later/ |website=Climbing |accessdate=4 June 2020}}</ref>

== Acquiring and manufacturing climbing gear ==
In the early 1950s, most American climbers imported climbing equipment from Europe or acquired it from US Army surplus. Pitons from these sources were made of mild steel that twisted and became unusable after only a few placements. Gallwas recognized the problem and was among the first to make and use heat-treated chrome-molybdenum steel alloy pitons. He patterned his pitons after John Salathé's so they could be placed hundreds of times without twisting. These improved pitons proved instrumental to the success of the first ascent of the Northwest Face of Half Dome in 1957.<ref name="Isserman"/>{{rp|312}}<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chouinard |first1=Yvon |title=Modern Yosemite Climbing |url=http://publications.americanalpineclub.org/articles/12196331900/Modern-Yosemite-Climbing |website=The American Alpine Club |accessdate=4 June 2020}}</ref> That same year, [[Yvon Chouinard]] began to produce and sell alloy-steel pitons. Chouinard's success with his pitons led him to establish Chouinard Equipment, Ltd, which later became [[Black Diamond Equipment]], Ltd.<ref name="Powell">{{cite book |last1=Powell |first1=Mark |last2=Gifford |first2=Jonathan |title=The five principles of performance thinking : the mindsets and techniques for success in the modern world |date=May 2, 2019 |publisher=LID Publishing |isbn=9781912555130 |pages=175 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k3qYDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT175 |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref>

* 1953 2nd ascent Yosemite Point Buttress. (With Royal Robbins)
* 1953 2nd ascent North Face [[Sentinel Rock]]. (With Royal Robbins and Don Wilson)<ref name="Isserman"/>{{rp|311}}
* 1953 Palisades Traverse [[Thunderbolt Peak]] to [[Mount Sill]] via [[North Palisade]]. (With [[Gary Hemming]])
* 1954 5th ascent Lost Arrow Spire. (With Wayne Merry)
* 1955 3rd ascent Lost Arrow Chimney. (With Charles Wilts and Don Wilson)
* 1956 1st ascent [[Canyon de Chelly National Monument|Spider Rock]], Canyon de Chelly National Monument, AZ, USA, March 30. (With Mark Powell and Don Wilson)<ref>The Mugelnoos, No. 280, p. 2, April 12, 1956</ref><ref>Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 42, No. 6, pp.45-49, June 1957</ref>
* 1956 1st ascent East Buttress of [[Middle Cathedral Rock]], Yosemite National Park, CA, USA,  June 16. (With Mark Powell and Don Wilson)<ref>The Mugelnoos, No.283, p. 4, July 12, 1956</ref><ref>Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 42, No. 6, p. 59, June 1957</ref>
* 1956 5th ascent [[Castle Rock Spire]]. (With Charles Wilts)
* 1956 1st ascent Cleopatra's Needle, Valley of the Thundering Water, NM, USA, September 6. (With Mark Powell and Don Wilson)<ref>Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 42, No. 6, pp. 63-64, June, 1957</ref><ref>The Mugelnoos, No. 286, p. 3, October 11, 1956</ref>
* 1957 1st ascent The Step, [[Tahquitz Rock|Tahquitz]] Idyllwild, CA, USA, May 18. (With Royal Robbins)<ref>The Mugelnoos, No. 294, p. 3, June 13, 1957</ref>
* 1957 1st ascent [[Totem Pole (Monument Valley)|Totem Pole]], Monument Valley, AZ, USA.  June 13. (With Bill Feuerer, Mark Powell, and Don Wilson)<ref>Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 43, No. 9, p. 72, November 1958</ref><ref>Summit Magazine, April, pp. 8-11, 1958</ref>
* 1957 1st ascent Northwest Face of [[Half Dome]], Yosemite, CA, USA, June 23–27. First grade VI climb in America. (With Mike Sherrick and Royal Robbins)<ref>The Muglenoos, No. 295, July 11, 1957</ref><ref>The Muglenoos, No. 297, p.4, September 12, 1957</ref><ref>Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 42, No. 10, pp. 12-13, December 1957</ref><ref>Sierra Club Bulletin, Vol. 43, No. 9, pp. 19-23, November 1958</ref><ref>T. Adler Books (2013), California Surfing and Climbing in the Fifties, tadlerbooks.com, Distributed Art Publishers,  p.67, {{ISBN|978-1-938922-26-8}}</ref>

== Business career ==
Gallwas studied chemistry at [[San Diego State University]].<ref name="AACC">{{cite web |title=Gerald Gallwas 1993 Outstanding Contributions through Service to the Profession of Clinical Chemistry |date= 1993 |url=https://www.aacc.org/community/awards/hall-of-fame/bios/a-to-k/gerald-gallwas |website=American Association for Clinical Chemistry |accessdate=4 June 2020}}</ref> He later ran a clinical chemistry laboratory while serving in the Army Medical Corps.<ref name="Jaehnig">{{cite web |last1=Jaehnig |first1=Kenton G. |title=Beckman Historical Collection002Finding aid created and encoded into EAD |url=https://findingaids.library.upenn.edu/records/SCIHIST_2012.002 |website=PACSCL |publisher=Science History Institute |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref> In 1964, he went on to work in diagnostics for scientific instrument maker [[Beckman Instruments]], Inc. In 1972, Gallwas served as a spokesperson for the adoption of voluntary consensus standards for laboratory medicine as the [[Food and Drug Administration]] began to regulate the medical device industry. Gallwas served on the board of directors of the National Committee for Clinical Laboratory Standards, now the [[Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute|Clinical Laboratory Standards Institute]] for ten years and was its president from 1982 to 1984.<ref name="AACC"/>

== Philanthropy ==
Gallwas met Beckman Instruments founder Dr. [[Arnold Beckman]] and his wife, Mabel, within a few weeks of joining the company. Their friendship led to Gallwas' 40-year affiliation with the Arnold and Mabel Beckman Foundation. Gallwas is credited with collecting and displaying Arnold Beckman's earliest inventions that helped launch the electronic revolution in the chemical and biological sciences. The inventions are displayed at the Arnold and Mabel Beckman Center of the National Academies of Science and Engineering in Irvine, CA. Additional exhibits that Gallwas collected are housed at the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]], now the Science History Institute in Philadelphia and at the [[Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology]] at the [[University of Illinois]] at Urbana Champaign.<ref>Thackray, Arnold and Meyers Jr., Minor, Arnold O. Beckman One Hundred Years of Excellence, Chemical Heritage Foundation, Philadelphia 2000, {{ISBN|0-941901-23-8}}.</ref>
